import time
from opentelemetry import trace
from prometheus_client import Histogram, Gauge

tracer = trace.get_tracer("vector-db")

embedding_latency = Histogram(
    "vector_db_embedding_latency_ms",
    "Embedding model call latency",
    buckets=[50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000]
)
query_latency = Histogram(
    "vector_db_query_latency_ms",
    "ANN search latency",
    buckets=[5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 250, 500]
)
embedding_version_gauge = Gauge(
    "vector_db_embedding_model_version",
    "Embedding model version in use",
    labelnames=["index_name"]
)

def instrumented_search(index, query: str, top_k: int = 5) -> list:
    with tracer.start_as_current_span("vector_db.search") as span:
        # Embed query
        t0 = time.time()
        query_embedding, embed_model_version = embed(query)
        embed_ms = (time.time() - t0) * 1000
        embedding_latency.observe(embed_ms)
        span.set_attribute("embedding.model_version", embed_model_version)
        span.set_attribute("embedding.latency_ms", embed_ms)

        # Search
        t1 = time.time()
        results = index.query(query_embedding, top_k=top_k)
        search_ms = (time.time() - t1) * 1000
        query_latency.observe(search_ms)

        span.set_attribute("search.top_k", top_k)
        span.set_attribute("search.max_score", results[0].score if results else 0)
        span.set_attribute("search.latency_ms", search_ms)
        return results

words.etymology: Vector from Latin vector, 'carrier'; DB abbreviation of database; observability from Latin observare. The compound emerged as RAG and semantic search systems moved to production and teams needed to reason about the correctness, not just the availability, of their retrieval layers.

words.shortDefinition: A structured review of an event that had the conditions for a serious incident but did not result in user-facing impact, documenting why the defenses held and what would happen if they fail next time.
words.simpleDefinition: A near-miss postmortem is written for events where nothing went wrong — a deployment caught in staging, an alert firing at 80% capacity before 100%, a bug found in shadow traffic before full rollout. Near-miss postmortems are high-leverage precisely because they offer full evidence without user impact. Throwing away that learning because 'nothing broke' is wasting the most valuable kind of incident data.
words.longDefinition: Near-misses are systematically under-documented because the psychological driver is clear: nothing went wrong, users were unaffected, the incident never made it to the status page. Writing a postmortem for something that didn't happen requires deliberate organizational policy. The case comes from safety engineering: Heinrich's Triangle (and subsequent safety research) proposes a ratio between minor incidents, near-misses, and serious accidents. The directional insight holds even if the exact ratios are contested: a near-miss is evidence that the system's contributing factors were present and the defenses held — barely. Documenting why the defenses held is as important as documenting when they fail. Examples worth a near-miss postmortem: a database migration script that would have deleted production data, caught in staging pre-flight; a feature flag rollout reaching 5% of users before a bug was detected and rolled back; CPU utilization reaching 92% before an on-call engineer noticed an anomaly in a dashboard that wasn't alerting; an expiring certificate caught by a synthetic monitor two hours before expiry. Near-miss postmortems are lighter-weight — they do not require full timeline reconstruction if the event was brief. Required sections: what happened, what caught it, why did the catch work, what would have happened if the catch failed, and what can be hardened.
words.connector: Think of near-miss postmortems like analyzing a car that almost skidded on ice but didn't — the driver braked in time. You want to understand why the brakes worked, why the driver noticed the ice, and whether either of those could fail next time.
words.techContext: The near-miss postmortem for the almost-deleted production table identified that the staging pre-flight check was the only defense — there was no dry-run mode on the migration tool and no separate review step. Two action items resulted: add dry-run validation and require a second engineer to approve any migration touching tables larger than 1M rows.
words.exampleSentence: The near-miss postmortem revealed that the certificate renewal alert was set to fire at 7 days remaining, but the manual renewal process took 9 days — a gap that would have caused an outage if the near-miss had not surfaced the scheduling conflict.
words.etymology: Near from Old English neah, 'close'; miss from Old English missan, 'to fail to hit'; postmortem from Latin post mortem, 'after death.' The compound near-miss postmortem emerged in SRE culture from aviation's near-miss reporting systems (NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System, ASRS), adapted to software operations in the 2010s.

words.shortDefinition: An on-call staffing model where incident response responsibility transfers between geographically distributed teams throughout the day so that every shift falls during normal business hours for the team holding it.
words.simpleDefinition: Follow-the-sun rotation eliminates the 3 AM page by ensuring on-call responsibility always rests with a team for whom it is currently daytime. A US team hands off to a team in Asia-Pacific as US business hours end; APAC hands off to EMEA; EMEA hands off back to US. Each team covers their own business hours, and no team carries overnight burden.
words.longDefinition: Follow-the-sun is an on-call staffing model designed to eliminate the health and quality-of-response costs of overnight paging by ensuring that the team holding incident response responsibility is always working within normal business hours. The handoff structure works as geographic bands: an Americas-based team holds on-call during Americas business hours, hands off to an APAC team as Americas business hours close, APAC hands off to EMEA, and EMEA hands off back to Americas. Each team covers approximately eight hours of their own daytime. The model requires: clearly defined handoff procedures (the same as shift handoffs during extended incidents — current state, what has been tried, current best theory, constraints, next actions), sufficient headcount in each geography to staff the rotation without overloading any individual team, a shared runbook and tooling infrastructure that any geography can operate without needing to wake up the off-hours team, and consistent incident documentation so the incoming team can catch up from the shared incident record. The primary challenges are handoff fidelity (the handoff must convey the incident state completely — a poor handoff turns a follow-the-sun strength into a weakness) and staffing imbalance (not all organizations have equivalent engineering depth in each time zone, which can create uneven on-call burden). It is most commonly used in large organizations with distributed engineering functions.
words.connector: Think of follow-the-sun rotation like a relay race run around the globe — each runner carries the baton through their own segment in daylight, passing it cleanly to the next runner before nightfall.
words.techContext: After implementing follow-the-sun rotation, the mean time to acknowledge a SEV-1 improved from 8 minutes (with overnight pages often answered by groggy engineers) to 3 minutes, as the team responding was always mid-shift and fully alert.
words.exampleSentence: Follow-the-sun rotation eliminated the 3 AM pages for the US team, but the first live handoff during a real incident revealed that the APAC team's runbook access was blocked by VPN restrictions that only applied outside North America.
words.etymology: Follow the sun from the idiomatic expression describing eastward travel that keeps pace with daylight. Rotation from Latin rotatio, 'a turning.' The compound is an operations management term that entered SRE vocabulary from global IT service desk practices in the 1990s-2000s.

words.shortDefinition: A classification assigned to an incident that determines who is paged, how quickly communications must go out, and how much organizational attention the incident warrants.
words.simpleDefinition: Severity levels (SEV-1 through SEV-5) are the shared language of incident response: SEV-1 means complete outage, all hands, executive escalation, status page within 5 minutes; SEV-5 means cosmetic issue, handle in business hours. They should be declared early based on user impact, upgraded immediately if the situation worsens, and serve as a forcing function for communications timing and escalation decisions.
words.longDefinition: Most organizations define three to five severity levels with a consistent pattern: the lowest number is the highest severity. The level determines escalation, response SLAs, and communications requirements. A typical matrix: SEV-1 (Critical) — complete outage of a critical service, or major data loss/corruption risk; all hands, IC activated, executive escalation, status page within 5 minutes. SEV-2 (Major) — significant degradation affecting a large user percentage, IC activated, status page updated. SEV-3 (Moderate) — partial degradation of a non-critical feature with a workaround; on-call team, internal notice only. SEV-4/SEV-5 (Minor) — cosmetic issues, single-user reports, no user impact; handled during business hours. Severity can be upgraded or downgraded as the incident evolves — upgrading is the IC's decision and does not require consensus. The most common severity error is under-declaring: calling a SEV-1 a SEV-2 to avoid higher escalation overhead, delaying executive awareness and customer communications precisely when speed matters most. When in doubt, start at the higher severity and downgrade once the situation is better understood. Some organizations track incident declaration rates as a positive metric — a high declaration rate means the team has a low barrier to coordination, which typically correlates with faster time to mitigation.
words.connector: Think of severity levels like a hospital triage system — a P1 trauma patient goes straight to the OR while a P5 sprained ankle waits in the waiting room. The level is not an evaluation of importance; it is a protocol trigger that routes the right resources to the right problem at the right speed.
words.techContext: The IC upgraded the incident from SEV-2 to SEV-1 at 14:31 when data confirmed that checkout failures were affecting all paid users, not just 20% — the upgrade immediately activated the executive escalation path and shifted the status-page update cadence from 30 minutes to 15 minutes.
words.exampleSentence: Declaring at the correct severity level on the first call saved 20 minutes of response time — the SEV-1 declaration immediately brought in the Comms Lead and opened the bridge call, whereas a SEV-2 would have left the on-call engineer handling everything alone.
words.etymology: Severity from Latin severitas, 'seriousness, strictness'; level from Old French livel, 'a measuring instrument.' The compound entered software operations from ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure Library) service management practices, where incident priority levels were a formal classification. Google and PagerDuty adapted the SEV-N convention.

words.shortDefinition: The single coordination channel — one Slack room or one bridge call — where all communication, investigation updates, decisions, and commands for an incident flow, preventing the fragmentation that extends incident duration.
words.simpleDefinition: The war room is the one channel where the incident lives. All decisions made outside it vanish from the incident timeline. Fragmented coordination across multiple channels — side DMs, separate calls, different Slack threads — is one of the most reliable ways to extend an incident duration. The IC controls the war room, limits who speaks, and keeps a running pinned status so any responder joining mid-incident can catch up by reading backward.
words.longDefinition: The war room is the canonical place where the incident happens. Its goal is legibility: a responder arriving 30 minutes into a SEV-1 should be able to read the channel backlog and understand the current situation without asking anyone for a briefing. War room hygiene rules: one channel per incident (create a dedicated Slack channel like #inc-2024-01-15-checkout at declaration time — do not run the incident in an existing team channel where context gets lost); minimize noise (the war room is not a brainstorm channel — the IC controls the agenda, off-topic hypotheses and status inquiries from uninvolved parties are redirected out); keep a running status line pinned to the channel (current severity, current best hypothesis, what is being tried, ETA for next update — this reduces the 'what's happening' interruptions); no side channels for decisions (anything decided in a DM or a side call that affects the incident must be posted back to the war room immediately, otherwise it vanishes from the timeline); and manage observers (leadership and curious engineers should mute and read, not post — helpful commentary from non-responders is a cognitive load tax on the people doing the work). Some organizations use a physical war room for colocated teams on extended SEV-1s. The same hygiene rules apply: one conversation at a time, IC controls who speaks, side conversations happen outside the room.
words.connector: Think of the war room like a surgical theater — only the people needed for the operation are at the table, there is one lead surgeon giving directions, and observers watch from the gallery above without interrupting. Everything critical happens in one place, clearly.
words.techContext: The post-incident review identified that the extended incident duration was partly caused by two engineers making a critical mitigation decision in a side DM and not posting it to the war room for 20 minutes — the IC and scribe had no record of it, leading to duplicated investigation work.
words.exampleSentence: The war room discipline paid off during the 4-hour SEV-1: because every decision was posted to the channel, the incoming IC on shift handoff could read the last 30 messages and be fully oriented in under 3 minutes without a live briefing.
words.etymology: War room originally referred to a military command center where battle decisions were made, maps were maintained, and officers coordinated operations — particularly common in WWII usage. Adopted metaphorically by IT operations in the 1990s and formalized in SRE incident response practices.

words.shortDefinition: Automated systems that detect a known failure condition and execute a predefined corrective action — restarting a crashed process, scaling up capacity, or rolling back a bad deployment — without human intervention.
words.simpleDefinition: Auto-remediation replaces the human in the loop for well-understood, deterministic failure patterns: if memory usage exceeds 90% for five minutes, restart the service; if the deployment error rate spikes above 5% in the first ten minutes, automatically roll back. It reduces MTTR for known failure classes and eliminates the toil of manual responses to predictable incidents.
words.longDefinition: Auto-remediation operationalizes the SRE toil-reduction principle: if a human can follow a runbook to fix a known problem, an automated system can execute the same steps faster and more reliably. It requires three prerequisites: a reliable detection signal (an alert or metric threshold that correctly identifies the failure condition with low false-positive rate), a safe, deterministic action (the remediation must not make the situation worse — rollbacks and restarts are generally safe; more complex database or network changes require careful safety analysis), and a bounded blast radius (the automated action should affect only the failing component, not healthy neighbors). Common patterns: process restart on OOM kill (detect via memory metrics or container exit code, restart with exponential backoff), deployment rollback on error-rate spike (detect via error budget burn rate, roll back to previous version automatically if the spike occurs within 15 minutes of deployment), and autoscaling on queue depth or CPU (detect saturation, add capacity within pre-defined limits). Auto-remediation is most valuable when paired with toil tracking — automating the incidents that appear most frequently in toil logs. The risk is over-automation: auto-remediating without understanding root cause can mask symptoms of a deeper failure, leading to a system that restarts continuously without ever surfacing the underlying problem. Circuit-breaker logic on the auto-remediation itself prevents runaway loops.
words.connector: Think of auto-remediation like a thermostat — it detects that the temperature has deviated from the set point and takes a predefined corrective action automatically, without requiring a person to manually adjust the heating every time the room gets cold.
words.techContext: Auto-remediation for the payment-service OOM pattern reduced mean time to recovery from 12 minutes (alert → page → on-call responds → restart) to 45 seconds (metric threshold → automatic container restart), eliminating the most frequent source of overnight pages for the team.
words.exampleSentence: Auto-remediation masked a memory leak for three weeks — the service kept restarting automatically and staying within SLO, so the underlying leak was invisible until toil tracking showed the restart rate trending upward on the weekly report.

# Kubernetes auto-remediation via liveness probe + restart policy
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: payment-service
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: payment-service
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: 8080
            initialDelaySeconds: 30
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3     # restart after 3 consecutive failures
          resources:
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi        # OOM kill threshold
      restartPolicy: Always
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0
      maxSurge: 1

The compound entered IT operations vocabulary from IT service management and SRE toil-reduction practices, particularly as infrastructure-as-code and Kubernetes made automated healing patterns feasible at scale.

words.shortDefinition: Chaos experiments run against real production traffic with tightly controlled blast radius, providing the most accurate resilience signal because staging environments cannot replicate production traffic patterns, data volumes, or dependency behavior.
words.simpleDefinition: Production chaos is the practice of running failure-injection experiments against real production infrastructure — at minimal scope — because staging environments lie. Staging traffic is synthetic, staging databases are smaller, and staging dependencies often behave differently. The gap between staging resilience and production resilience is only visible in production. The blast-radius controls that make this safe are small traffic percentages, off-peak timing, and automatic rollback on steady-state violation.
words.longDefinition: The realism gap between staging and production is the central tension in chaos engineering practice. Staging environments get several things wrong: traffic patterns (synthetic traffic does not represent real burst patterns, tail latency, and concurrency), data volume (staging databases are typically smaller, so failures that emerge from large dataset behavior — slow queries, index misses at scale — do not manifest), dependency behavior (staging dependencies are often stubbed or point to separate staging versions), and infrastructure configuration (staging clusters are often smaller — a node-drain on a 3-node cluster is not the same experiment as on a 150-node cluster). Strategies for managing production chaos safely: dark traffic replay (mirror production traffic to a shadow cluster where experiments run without affecting real users), traffic percentage targeting (experiment against 1% of production traffic via feature flags or load-balancer rules), off-peak scheduling (run experiments during low-traffic windows), and canary instance targeting (run experiments only against the canary deployment slice). Staging-only chaos programs create false security — they validate staging environment resilience, not production resilience. The principlesofchaos.org manifesto's third principle is 'run experiments in production,' explicitly acknowledging that staging-only validation is insufficient, while the fifth principle ('minimize blast radius') provides the safety constraint.
words.connector: Think of production chaos like drug trials — you test in controlled lab conditions first (staging), but the drug is only approved based on real-world trials in humans (production), because lab conditions cannot fully replicate human biology. The controlled scope of the trial is what makes real-world testing safe.
words.techContext: The team graduated from staging chaos to production chaos by starting with 1% traffic targeting and off-peak scheduling, discovering that the payment service's connection pool exhausted under real Black Friday-level traffic patterns even though it handled synthetic load tests without issue.
words.exampleSentence: Production chaos exposed a failure mode that three months of staging experiments had completely missed: under real production data volumes, the database query optimizer chose a different execution plan that caused connection timeouts at rates synthetic benchmarks never triggered.
words.etymology: Production from Latin productio, 'a leading forward'; chaos from Greek khaos. The compound production chaos emerged from the Netflix/principlesofchaos.org tradition to distinguish experiments run against live user traffic from those run in isolated environments.

words.shortDefinition: The structured distributed trace produced by an LLM agent's execution — a tree of alternating reasoning spans and tool-call spans with variable depth, session-level aggregate attributes, and retry markers.
words.simpleDefinition: A multi-step agent trace looks nothing like a microservice waterfall. It is a tree: root span carries session totals (steps, tokens, cost, outcome), and the children are alternating LLM-reasoning spans and tool-call spans. Depth varies at runtime based on what the agent finds — the same task can take 3 steps or 15. Standard OTel backends can store the spans but need the GenAI semantic conventions to render them as agent traces rather than flat waterfalls.
words.longDefinition: The ReAct pattern (Reason + Act) is the dominant execution pattern for LLM agents. Each step is: Think → Act (tool call) → Observe (tool result) → Think → Act → ... → Answer. This produces a trace shape fundamentally different from a microservice trace. Key structural differences: variable depth (the same task takes 3 steps or 15 depending on what the agent finds — trace depth is determined by runtime behavior, not code structure), alternating span types (LLM reasoning spans and tool-call spans have different attributes and performance profiles and must be visualized and queried separately), and session-level aggregates (total steps, total tokens, total cost, and outcome are attributes of the root span, aggregated across all children — they cannot be derived from any single child span). The root span should carry: task_id, user_id, total_steps, total_tokens, total_cost, wall_time, and outcome (success, failure, timeout, stuck_in_loop). Each LLM reasoning span carries: model, prompt tokens, completion tokens, TTFT, prompt version. Each tool-call span carries: tool name, input parameters, output, latency, success flag, retry flag. LangSmith, LangFuse, and Arize Phoenix render agent traces as trees rather than linear waterfalls. Standard OTel backends like Jaeger and Tempo can store the spans but lack native agent-trace visualization — the GenAI semantic conventions work under the CNCF OTel SIG AI/ML working group is partially motivated by enabling generic backends to render these traces correctly.
words.connector: Think of a multi-step agent trace like a detective's case file — not a single report but a growing dossier of observations, interviews (tool calls), and reasoning steps. The root 'case' carries the summary; each page is a step in the investigation.
words.techContext: The multi-step agent trace exposed that research agent sessions failing with 'incomplete result' had a consistent pattern: step_8 was always a retry of the same web_search query that returned zero results, causing the agent to loop rather than conclude — a tool-side fix (adding a fallback search provider) resolved it.
words.exampleSentence: Multi-step agent traces revealed that the P95 steps-to-completion distribution had shifted from 8 to 22 steps after a model update — the agent was second-guessing its own tool outputs and adding redundant verification steps that the previous model had not exhibited.

words.shortDefinition: A service-level indicator for AI-augmented systems that extends the classical latency-and-availability model with quality scores and cost metrics as first-class signals, forming a three-dimensional SLO triplet.
words.simpleDefinition: An AI service has three dials, not two: latency, quality, and cost. All three need SLOs. A system that hits its latency SLO using a cheaper model may breach its quality SLO; one that hits its quality SLO by using a larger model may breach its cost SLO. The AI-era SLI triplet makes these trade-offs explicit and alerts on each dimension independently.
words.longDefinition: Traditional SLIs map well to deterministic services: availability (is it up?), latency (is it fast?), and error rate (is it correct?). Error rate is binary — either the request succeeded or it failed. For LLM-augmented services, success is a spectrum, and the traditional SLI triplet is insufficient. The AI-era SLI triplet: Latency SLO (split into TTFT and end-to-end latency; example: P95 TTFT < 2s AND P95 end-to-end < 20s for responses under 1000 tokens; measured separately per model tier since fast models and reasoning models have different latency profiles); Quality SLO (a continuous quality score from eval-as-observability must stay above a threshold; example: rolling 1-hour P50 relevance score > 0.72, groundedness score > 0.80; measured on sampled production traffic via async evals; breaching the quality SLO triggers an alert and typically initiates a prompt rollback investigation); Cost SLO (average cost per request and total daily cost within budget envelopes; example: average cost per request < $0.008, daily cost < $500; a cost SLO breach signals a budget incident before the monthly invoice arrives). Error budget accounting in the AI era extends the traditional model: quality budget (hours of quality SLO violation per rolling 30-day window), cost budget (monthly LLM spend vs. allocation), and hallucination budget (maximum acceptable fraction of low-groundedness responses before a human review gate activates). The three SLIs are not independent — a system under load may sacrifice quality to preserve latency; a system that caches aggressively reduces cost but drifts toward stale responses. Making these trade-offs explicit in dashboards is the engineering discipline of AI-era reliability.
words.connector: Think of AI-era SLIs like a restaurant health inspection expanded to cover food safety (quality), wait time (latency), and food cost (cost) as equally weighted pass/fail criteria — a restaurant that passes on speed but fails on food safety is still failing the inspection.
words.techContext: The AI-era SLI dashboard surfaces all three dimensions simultaneously: TTFT P95, groundedness score P50, and daily cost trend. When the model provider silently promoted a new checkpoint, the groundedness SLO fired 40 minutes before any user complaint — the team rolled back the model version before the quality degradation reached the majority of users.
words.exampleSentence: The AI-era SLI triplet made the engineering trade-off explicit: switching to the smaller model tier preserved the cost SLO and the latency SLO but immediately breached the quality SLO — a data-driven decision that required all three dials to be visible simultaneously.

codeExample.code:
# Prometheus alerting rules for AI-era SLI triplet
groups:
  - name: ai_era_slos
    rules:
      # 1. Latency SLO — TTFT
      - alert: LLM_TTFT_SLOBreach
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            rate(gen_ai_ttft_ms_bucket[5m])
          ) > 2000
        for: 3m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "P95 TTFT > 2s (AI latency SLO breach)"

      # 2. Quality SLO — groundedness
      - alert: LLM_GroundednessSLOBreach
        expr: |
          avg_over_time(llm_quality_score{eval_type="groundedness"}[1h]) < 0.80
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: page
        annotations:
          summary: "Rolling 1h groundedness score < 0.80 (quality SLO breach)"

      # 3. Cost SLO — daily budget
      - alert: LLM_CostBudgetBreach
        expr: llm_daily_cost_usd_total{environment="production"} > 500
        labels:
          severity: warning
        annotations:
          summary: "Daily LLM cost exceeded $500 budget envelope"

words.etymology: AI abbreviation of Artificial Intelligence; era from Latin aera, 'an age, epoch'; SLI abbreviation of Service Level Indicator, coined in Google's SRE Book (2016). The compound AI-era SLI emerged around 2024 as production AI systems required extending the classical SRE reliability framework with quality and cost dimensions.
